I'm having codex put together a nice little architecture viewer for my clojure projects.  It was all going very well.  I was doing other things with other agents, but had one agent dedicated to the viewer and I'd type in a prompt every once in awhile.  

Several hours later I notice that codex was struggling.  I'd ask it to fix X and it would break Y.  So I asked it if cleaning up the code would help.  It told me, in no uncertain terms, that it was having a lot of trouble keeping everything straight.

So I told it to break the system into pieces, separate UI from non UI and put them in isolated directories.  Now I'm using the crap tool to break the functions up into easily consumable chunks, and vastly increase the test coverage.  

Then I'll use the mutate tool to further enhance the coverage so that it will find it very difficult to break existing behavior.

results.text:
Once I got involved in guiding the architecture, all the pieces fell into place.  I have a nice layered architecture now, with dependencies all well managed.  I built a tool to check those dependencies on every test run.  I also built a tool to help me visualize the architecture.  

Conclusion: Architecture remains, so far, in the realm of human judgement.  AIs, as intelligent and insightful as they appear to be, do not have that level of insight and judgement.  

Bottom line: Don't trust the AIs to create the architecture.  They'll just muddy the waters.

results.text:
The architecture experiment was very revealing.  In an attempt to create a mathematically conformant architecture codex ripped the code to smithereens and put all manner of ports and adapters in place while sharding up the source files like a buzz saw.  

Remarkably, the tests all kept passing and playtesting showed no problems.

Claude then reviewed and gently suggested different options.  I felt like I was flying blind, so I had codex write me up an architecture viewer that allows me to see the high levels, drill down to lower levels, and even see the code. 

Then Claude and I had a very long talk about the nature of the architecture.  It made a number of suggestions, but none of them satisfied me.  So, in frustration,  I proposed an architecture to Claude.  It was a very simple layered approach:

UI->Turn Management->(Player | Computer)->shared-mechanics->(state | config).  7 Components, with precisely defined dependencies.

From there we iterated through a set of issues and questions until the plan solidified.
